The AGMAI guidance was mainly about responsible release of informal proofs and subsequent support of building understanding of those proofs, with discussion of formalization limited to certain technical requirements (including "It would be helpful to include machine-readable metadata correlating the natural language and formal artifacts.", which seems to apply to the point above about not clearly saying which theorems in which PDFs are formalized). I suggest, however, that something analogous to "Step II: Supporting human understanding" should also apply to digestion of formal proofs.

For informal material that's new, this would necessarily be dependent on, but could also contribute to, understanding of those proofs. For informal material from the existing literature that's a dependency of the new proofs, the extent to which particular material gets used across many different formalizations should help indicate what should be a priority to push upstream as far as possible (increasing quality and generality along the way) to avoid needing large numbers of patched dependencies in future. (Though patched dependencies are certainly better than "AI copies existing repository, deleting all attribution as it does so" which has also been known in some other formalizations.)

For informal results that don't have corresponding formalizations, meanwhile, information about why they don't have formalizations (supposing, in many cases, it's large missing dependencies) might also indicate areas to support the building and upstreaming of formal libraries.

The only one where I've commented externally on the mathematical content is 155 (A translational tile with no fully periodic tiling in dimension three). Since my comments were on a Google group whose archives are only visible to members, a brief summary:

  • The claimed result (like the Greenfeld-Tao work it builds on) is weakly aperiodic (no tiling with a three-dimensional lattice of translations), not strongly aperiodic (no tiling with any translations as symmetry), but the paper doesn't actually mention the "weak" and "strong" terms used for this distinction in the literature at all (it doesn't do a good job of discussing the more general background).
  • While it mentions incidentally that the tile is probably not connected ("The result concerns full periodicity; neither connectedness of the tile nor absence of every individual nonzero period is asserted."), it doesn't refer to the Greenfeld-Kolountzakis work on how to go from a disconnected translational tile to a connected one at the cost of two extra dimensions. In fact it turns out to be not too hard to turn a disconnected translational tile in Z3\mathbb{Z}^3Z3 into a connected one without needing the extra dimensions (so there is weak aperiodicity for a connected translational tile in Z3\mathbb{Z}^3Z3 and thus R3\mathbb{R}^3R3, not just Z5\mathbb{Z}^5Z5 and R5\mathbb{R}^5R5 which would follow directly from this paper together with Greenfeld-Kolountzakis).

I'd like to alert people that several of the comparator challenges are noticeably broken and hackable. Afaik this hasn't been talked about elsewhere yet. The issue is that many definitions that should be treated as fixed are given in the definition_names field of the .json, meaning they can be freely overridden. For instance, in EuclideanFiveColor.lean, the entire content is just

def ProperColoring (colorCount : ℕ) (coloring : ℂ → Fin colorCount) : Prop :=
  ∀ point otherPoint : ℂ, ‖point - otherPoint‖ = 1 → coloring point ≠ coloring otherPoint

theorem no_proper_five_coloring : ¬ ∃ coloring : ℂ → Fin 5, ProperColoring 5 coloring := by
  sorry

At the same time, the .json lists:

  "theorem_names": [
    "OAI.EuclideanFiveColor.no_proper_five_coloring"
  ],
  "definition_names": [
    "OAI.EuclideanFiveColor.ProperColoring"
  ],

meaning that the definition of ProperColoring can be freely changed without affecting Comparator's acceptance. I confirmed that I can get Comparator to accept a broken variant of this proof, where all I need to prove is:

def ProperColoring (colorCount : ℕ) (coloring : ℂ → Fin colorCount) : Prop := False
theorem no_proper_five_coloring : ¬ ∃ coloring : ℂ → Fin 5, ProperColoring 5 coloring :=
  fun ⟨_, h⟩ => h

Now in this case, it's pretty straightforward to check that the definition is the right one, because it's right at the top of a file that imports only Mathlib. But there are 6 other cases where the Comparator file is similarly broken with a trivial proof:

  • Bernier .lean, .json
  • LogspaceEquality (that L=RL=BPL) .lean, .json
  • KServer .lean, .json
  • Naimark .lean, .json
  • OccupiedOverlap
  • Rokhlin
  • SpinAngle - this one has a legitimate sorry in a def, but it's a proof obligation, not a definitional hole to fill, and Comparator lets you freely change the rest of the definition; and besides there are two other definitions with no sorry still in the list.

Worth noting that ElementaryPositivity has a definitional hole but that's correct, they have a data-carrying term as their main objective instead of a Prop (fine).

I don't see any pattern in what was subject to this error, and often only a few definitions out of a large file are given this special, broken, treatment.

This issue also led me to looking at the Naimark one, and, small issue: the Comparator file really just shows that you can construct <some particular C* algebra with a prescribed property> in Lean under standard axioms. The frontier of mathematical knowledge before was that you could construct such algebras under ZFC with additional axioms, and the main point of the OAI result was that you could do it entirely within ZFC. Unfortunately, the Lean leaves open the possibility of relying nontrivially on the inaccessible cardinal axioms, which I would usually say is irrelevant but definitely knocks a chip off in this particular instance.

Regarding quality issues with the Lean code, see my remarks early in this discussion about how the AGMAI guidance talks about how releases of informal proofs should only be a start towards understanding, and how I think similar principles should apply to releases of formal proofs: the release of such material should only be a starting point towards getting it into high quality and (where known material rather than very specific to a particular result) integrated into reusable libraries of formalized mathematics, and that should be part of the responsibilities of AI companies releasing formalizations.

As a mathlib maximalist, I naturally think that should be getting things to mathlib quality and into mathlib, but for large quantities of material that would inevitably take a long time (OpenAI's release has 11 times as many lines of Lean as mathlib, though a fair amount may be specific to particular results, or junk that could be removed), so getting things to Tau Ceti quality and into Tau Ceti would be a plausible interim first step.

Maybe the Lean community should issue its own guidance, or suggest additions to AGMAI, on such issues with the lifecycle of releases of formalized material (and, possibly, on the levels of quality that should be achieved even in an initial release, beyond the formal points about comparator and formalization.yaml that are already in the AGMAI recommendations).

Philosophically, I interpret the way OpenAI seems to have treated the Lean release thus.

The theory-building / problem-solving dichotomy in mathematics is well-known. It has also been much discussed lately how cross-fertilization between the two is essential: theory-building suggests problems, while solving problems helps motivate both theory and further problems. (As has also been noted, human work on hard problems often involves many bits of incremental progress, published in their own papers, each of which can motivate both theory and problems even when it doesn't end up on the critical path to actual solutions of those problems - and since this release of papers only provides ten reasoning traces to go with hundreds of solutions, we don't know any of the interesting but discarded approaches to all the other problems that could have motivated other mathematics if developed by humans gradually over the course of years. While the academic incentive structure that says "publish a paper" is the most worthwhile thing to do with partial progress has its own problems, so does hiding all the ideas equivalent to what might be found in years of work.)

The AI approach to informal mathematics represents an unhealthy extreme of the problem-solving approach, valuing solving concrete problems chosen in advance above all else, and partial progress only being considered worthwhile if it's sufficiently strong (e.g. improving specified bounds) in a way specified in advance (probably - we have too few of the OpenAI prompts, and only extracts of those, to be able to tell what the rules were for surfacing partial progress), rather than more subjectively being considered interesting such as humans might think worthwhile to write a paper about. Furthermore, while humans care about how a problem was solved and what can be learned from the solution, for the AI it's much more about just claiming credit to be the first to solve something.

Something similar applies to formalized mathematics. For humans, using and especially contributing to mathlib encourages a theory-building viewpoint - even when working on formalizing problem-solving mathematics. I did my PhD a long time ago in problem-solving mathematics (indeed, an early draft had the word "problems" in its title, which I changed to "theory" on advice that that sounded more respectable). Contributing to mathlib helped give me a renewed appreciation of the theory-building side of mathematics. People often want to contribute to mathlib or other reusable libraries, and give back to the community they've benefited from, even if sometimes the ideas of beginners about what and how to contribute don't actually fit well into mathlib.

Just as the AIs are following an unhealthy extreme of the problem-solving approach to informal mathematics, so they are also following such an extreme to formal mathematics (but more so, in that humans doing large formalizations naturally tend a bit more to the theory-building side when doing so). Paying attention to all the little details in a human formalization naturally makes one think more of exactly how best to set things up and what the theory should look like; the size and complexity of such a formalization naturally makes one want to avoid junk that will make it harder to maintain; the time required to develop such a formalization (and the likelihood that one will end up wanting things that were added to mathlib after the formalization started) naturally means one cares about maintaining it during the development process. The AIs, being concerned with a one-off goal of being sorry-free and nothing else, never gain an appreciation of high quality formal theory building; never need to care about maintenance or making their code less cumbersome to work with; don't feel any sense of reciprocity that just as they've benefited from high-quality APIs existing formal libraries, so they should construct such APIs and give them back to such libraries to benefit the next user wanting to formalize something else in the same area (if anything, they might consider it an anti-goal to make things easier for a different AI company to formalize their solutions).

I see no reason why AIs should be incapable of good theory-building in either informal or formal mathematics, even if it's harder to precisely define what's good and so to give RL signals for it (there are plenty of examples of what was found over time to be good, and why). And where they do find something hard at present, a human-AI collaboration is a perfectly reasonable approach if you're not an AI company with a goal of eliminating human thought. But good theories and high-quality formalized library contributions don't make for sensationalized press releases and blog posts.

Been looking at the QRH stuff for several days now, and I think we're more or less stuck at the 7/8 boundary without better estimation techniques or estimates for higher moments. The thing that makes Eisenstein special is being an odd number of roots of unity means that reflected character and the completed character become quadratic the entire way through, whereas even roots of unity bring in higher order characters. But just being odd isn't enough, because 3 is the smallest non-degenerate case, everything about it is much simpler. Its zero detector, Mobius identity, singular value, etc. m = 5 and higher bring in branches that aren't cancelled (by this line of argument), so we still can't use the large quadratic sieve. And the large quadratic sieve + Cauchy-Schwarz + Gram bounds and taking absolute values end up throwing away enough signed information that 13/15 is the limit (better upper and lower bounds together are needed to lower that). So it's really taking advantage of the simplicity of the Eisenstein field and it's nice to eliminate Siegel zeros (which I needed for another project), but it's not the breakthrough that lets us prove the cancellation we really need to get all the way to RH.

The README says:

To establish a definition hole, the challenge must provide it as a sorried definition:

def large : Nat := sorry

theorem large_lt : 37 < large := sorry

All of the holes must then be put into the definition_names field in configuration.json:

{
    "challenge_module": "Challenge",
    "solution_module": "Solution",
    "theorem_names": ["large_lt"],
    "definition_names": ["large"],
    "permitted_axioms": ["propext", "Quot.sound", "Classical.choice"]
}

For all definition_names, comparator ensures that in the solution:

  • the name, type, universe levels and safety level match
  • the constant does not (transitively) refer to non-permitted axioms
  • the constant type checks
If I understand correctly, the theorem_names and definition_names follow the same logic, i.e. check the RHS of := have the desired type and with only permitted axioms.
Basically, definition_names list names of definitions that can be (re)defined in the Solution.lean.
